- He found this work fun and notes it is all OCGA work, about what the servers receive and send.

chunks.heading: Server performance fixes: JSON to protobuf
chunks.text:
- The first version of the event path used JSON to pass events.
- Encoding JSON alone "completely caved the game server".
- The fix was moving to protobufs, using Go zero-allocation (zero garbage generating) protobuf tooling. This helped the servers run well.
- He says it was not memory arenas, but "cool Go stuff" that avoids allocation.

chunks.heading: Next project at Netflix and working style
chunks.text:
- After one last data task, he moves to a project that involves React, but "subverting React" and making it "become not React".
- He will build an LSP for it, which means writing a lot of Rust and a lot of JavaScript.
- Working style: he did all of the Reggie and stats work alone, but worked with many people to get things out and running.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen walks through his gated six-phase LLM process: structs, interfaces, to-dos, implement-then-revert, invariants, then implement. He stays in control of the code, hand-edits instead of describing API changes in English, and builds a JSON game mode so agents can actually play and test the game.

chunks.heading: ThePrimeagen's six-phase planning workflow for programming with LLMs
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen built this workflow because he was traveling for two weeks with no keyboard and still wanted to produce the code he would normally write. He could run it from his phone (Cursor's preview app, iOS only) or his computer.
- He asks the LLM to go slowly, one step at a time, and he reviews and corrects each phase before moving on. The point is "slowly designing the thing one step at a time the way I would like to program it."
- Phase 0 (technically a seventh phase): research and come up with a plan for phases one through six.
- Phase 1, structs: define the data structures being built.
- Phase 2, interfaces: define the functions that need to be created or changed (the project's API surface).
- Phase 3, to-dos: place a to-do in every spot in the codebase where code needs to change. He checks that each to-do exists, adds missing ones, and removes ones he doesn't want.
- Phase 4, implement then revert: the LLM implements the change, runs the game in JSON mode to verify it plays through, undoes all the changes, and reports where it had to break from the structs, interfaces or to-dos.
- Phase 5, invariants: add any invariants. He says LLMs are "horrible at this step" and he hasn't figured out how to get them to do it well.
- Phase 6, implement the real change. His joke for phase 7 is "finishing a game is my goal."

chunks.heading: The gating rule: he decides when code advances
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen stays the one who determines when code is ready for the next step. If the data structures look wrong, "we do not go forward." Same for interfaces and to-dos.
- The test at phase 4 is: can the requested feature be implemented with the to-dos, data structures and interfaces without going anywhere else? If not, "break it again."
- He says phase 4 is his favorite step and "the greatest change in how I design my programs yet." Even without an AI, hand-coding the implementation and noting where the plan broke is "a great way to get information back."
- He says he usually doesn't just prompt "make me a game and make sure it's pretty good." His view: "agents left alone just produce" garbage, and simply telling AI to go do the thing wrecks a project.

chunks.heading: Giving LLMs a JSON mode to play and test the game
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen's tower-defense-style card game is written in Odin with raylib. He added a JSON mode (`odin run . -- --json`) that runs the full game but emits JSON instead of rendering, and accepts JSON events (mouse operations, moving cards) as input.
- He built it instead of an MCP server because he wanted something "more robust than MCP" that can also emit events. He compares it to a Playwright CLI for game dev.
- The game loop is deterministic: it uses a fixed test delta time and no real sleeping, so it can run at something like "40,000 frames a second," which makes testing very fast.
- In Cursor, he prompts it to play in JSON mode, place a tower and record every JSON output to a file so it can be replayed.
- Longer-term goal: a real agent loop where an agent plays as a character (the blacksmith) for 1,000 games, he inspects win percentages, and the agent writes a file of skills and best strategies, so he can see which cards win most and least.
- He admits he should document how to launch and control the game in an `agent.md`.
- He has few unit tests, only basic layout and animation tests. The JSON mode is his main verification path.

chunks.heading: Design example: static enemy array instead of a dynamic array
chunks.text:
- One PR he made through this process replaced a dynamic array of enemies with a fixed-size array, with a defined maximum number of enemies and no removals.
- Reason: during a level, a dead enemy still needs to play a death animation, so it must stay in the array to keep updating. Enemies are marked dead (with the time of death) or completed (path percent 100%) rather than removed.
- Each new wave clears out the previous enemies and projectiles.
- Draw loops iterate up to the enemy count and skip finished enemies. The same pattern applies to towers.
- He says this is the kind of design change the workflow handles well.

chunks.heading: Where LLMs fail him and what he does by hand
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen says he hates describing API changes in English. When reviewing, he'd rather make the edit himself because "I can just do it much much faster."
- Example: a mouse-interaction bug where he wanted a function to return the highest Z-ordered interactive element instead of doing the interaction inside the check. He tried to get agents to do it about seven times while traveling and couldn't get normal code. He hand-wrote it in about 15 minutes. His takeaway: "Some problems are just horrible to describe in English."
- He tried to have an LLM "slop" an MCP server into the project and calls the result "absolutely awful."
- LLMs keep using `println`-style `ln` calls in Odin even though they don't exist there.
- He says LLMs don't produce great code but produce even worse assets. He used a human pixel artist (Adam C. Younis) for the game art and hand-rolled his own immediate-mode animation system, which he's proud of.
- He admits a personal weakness: he's "not really great at reviewing code" and sometimes lets logic slip into the UI layer that belongs in the game layer, especially when reviewing on his phone.
- His framing: "Can I become a good programmer while using an LLM?" He wants to be deliberate about how he uses AI.

chunks.heading: "55": his local tooling for running the workflow with worktrees
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen built a Neovim-based tool called 55, named after the Halo BR55 battle rifle. It's the follow-up to his earlier AI Vim plugin 99 (named for the SRS99 sniper rifle). The name signals precision over "spray and pray."
- Each project (for example, "the damage" feature where an enemy reaching the end of the map deals one damage to the player) gets its own Git worktree, so it can hold pending changes without touching his main checkout.
- Starting a project: he tells the agent it will go through seven phases of planning and to acknowledge when ready, then gives the task. He can see which phase it is in, and whether an agent is running, from a home screen.
- The `inspect` command puts every Git hunk into the Vim quickfix list so he can walk through the agent's changes. A toggle shows diff lines.
- Workflow: let the agent make the change, then edit the code himself by hand, then continue the phases locally. For fixes he prompts directly, for example "pull from master and resolve conflicts" or "enemies no longer are removed but marked dead."
- Planned next step: a cloud handoff (a control-G command in 55 that records a handoff prompt). If he is partway through a change and has to leave, he can send it to the cloud and finish on his phone. He says he hasn't tested it and doesn't know if it's possible.

chunks.heading: Autocomplete, not vibe coding, and why 55 isn't public
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen says he is not vibe coding. He wants to stay the one doing the coding and the reviewing.
- For tab autocomplete he still uses Supermaven (not his own 99), citing about 250 ms latency. He says that if he's locked in and his program is clear in his head, he can go faster and better than any LLM, and autocomplete is enough.
- He released 99 as experimenting in public, but isn't releasing 55 yet because he isn't sure it's the right approach: "I don't know if 99's the right choice, so I want to first really like it."
- Game status: he intends to release it as a real game. An older Lua version (Mordoria, "V2") is public with a retained-mode UI. The new Odin version uses immediate mode for both UI and animations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen recounts how fear of falling behind while starting a company at 24 led to 24-hour coding binges and hurt his marriage. He argues the current "you'll be left behind" AI narrative is hype, and that steady daily progress, rest and deep craft beat chasing every new tool.

chunks.heading: "You won't fall behind": the fear of being left behind by AI is mostly a feeling, not reality
chunks.text:
- He says the experience isn't new, but today it is pressured by a new set of outcomes he didn't face when learning to program.
- His message: "You're not falling behind. And I do mean that."
- A viewer he quotes describes it well: it is the feeling of falling behind, not necessarily the reality. When models and tools change every few days, it creates a constant "I need to keep up" mentality that is "super toxic".

chunks.heading: Past hustle burnout: ThePrimeagen's 24-hour coding sessions at 24-25
chunks.text:
- At about 24-25, freshly married and trying to start a company, he programmed for over 24 hours straight, in a studio apartment next to the door while his wife slept.
- He loved programming, but he also had constant fear and anxiety that he was falling behind, wasn't outputting enough and wouldn't launch successfully.
- The anxiety colored his social life. With friends he kept thinking he had to get home because it was taking too long.
- He describes it as a kind of mental breakdown over a large period of his life. It caused undue stress for his wife, probably hurt his marriage for some time, and he calls it one of his more foolish moments. He also says he wasn't a great father in his kids' early years.
- His fear then came from real competitors and a startup race, not from a generalized "everyone will be left behind" narrative.
- He admits he still struggles to step away, calling it "such a learned or ingrained problem inside of me".

chunks.heading: Work hard, but taking time off won't change your life
chunks.text:
- He is not against working hard. He is a "huge proponent" of going all in, especially when young: "Two butt cheeks, whole ass that attempt."
- Becoming deeply competent and excellent at your craft is "an extremely rewarding thing".
- A good day is one where you learn and make a step forward. Taking a weekend off "is not going to dramatically change the course of your life".
- Being engaged and focused when it's time to work pays dividends. So does learning and understanding the underlying thing, rather than "pressing the I'm going to be lucky tonight button".
- His advice: choose the good things and the good work. "You don't have to keep up with everything."

chunks.heading: Tech hype cycles have always made newcomers anxious
chunks.text:
- He compares AI to earlier waves. People graduating in 2020-2021 or going through bootcamps felt an onslaught of technologies they had to learn or fall behind.
- Example: he argued on Twitter that React Server Components weren't a big deal. He said you don't need to switch your company over or sprinkle them on your resume. He says he still feels justified given the vulnerabilities that have surfaced since. People quote-tweeted him saying he gives the worst advice if you're not keeping up.
- He thinks this kind of pressure causes needless swirl and anxiety in people.

chunks.heading: Early AI tooling advice quickly became obsolete
chunks.text:
- When ChatGPT 3.5 came out, people said it was replacing them. During the ChatGPT 3.5 and Opus 3 / 3.5 era, the constant message was that if you weren't using these tools you'd be left behind.
- He argues that almost nothing people learned in that era is still useful. The way you set up context and interact with models today "looks almost nothing like it did in the beginning".
- Conclusion: chasing the latest and greatest workflow out of fear is wasted effort, since "every last single thing about that era is effectively void."

chunks.heading: Be skeptical of token-maxing and negative-valence AI hype
chunks.text:
- He agrees with George Hotz's post that "the constant [nonsense] about the window closing or the perpetual underclass or falling hopelessly behind" is "negative valence hype". It is untrue and mostly designed to make you feel bad about yourself.
- He also agrees with Hotz that the jump from "fancy autocomplete, smart compiler, better search engine" to "it's going to own the whole light cone" is a straw man.
- On incentives: AI companies make money when you "token max". He asks: "Don't you realize that there's a little bit of a perverse incentive when the people who are selling shovels [tell] you the only thing you ever need to practice or do is dig holes?"
- He is not saying don't investigate. He keeps a loop running to test whether the approach actually works or is a waste of time, because he wants an informed opinion. But he is "not betting everything on this" and is aware of the risk of spending too much money on it.
- He notes that nobody knows what the future holds right now: "I have no idea."

chunks.heading: Practical advice: use AI as a search engine and debugger, have fun, and keep building skill
chunks.text:
- He tells people to enjoy this period: you can build whatever you want and investigate whatever you want.
- He values AI as a fantastic search engine that works even with terrible English. Before, his options were Stack Overflow or reading the code.
- Example: he introduced a regression into a game he was building and asked the AI to launch `perf` and tell him which function he broke. About half an hour later it came back with exactly what he had done wrong. He calls that a big time saver.
- His closing view: learning and becoming better at your craft is still an excellent choice, as he said a couple of years ago and last year, and he doesn't think you're being left behind.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen reacts to a video on the cost of AI coding. He argues that infinite idea capacity without friction wears you down, that coding doubles as design thinking, and that going deep on one thing beats chasing everything. He also pushes back on AI FOMO and says to keep room for the programming you enjoy.

chunks.heading: Many ideas, little depth: why AI-assisted coding can drain energy
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen describes his past coding as flow: "the ideas in my head came alive and my fingers were the translation layer." He calls himself "a wizard at Vim."
- He says writing code was never the problem with AI. Bad code has always existed and is fixable. What he misses is sitting down and programming, and he accepts that this is becoming a dying activity, like horse riding.
- He still thinks the AI benefits are impossible to ignore. People can succeed without it, as some did writing code in Notepad, but the average person won't.
- He cites an old article's point: the most senior engineers can do the most junior tasks. They can plow through monotony, stay on task, and break hard problems into slog work. Learning to say no, handle the mundane and work through the slog was a big career level-up for him.
- Most programming is "put pipe A into pipe B," not building a compiler from first principles. His own card game is now mostly UI and game rules, so the hard part is generating ideas and playing it enough to see whether it is fun.

chunks.heading: Coding used to be design time, and AI removes that
chunks.text:
- Before AI, an idea took little time to conceive and about 10x to 100x longer to implement, even in a basic version.
- That implementation time doubled as design time. While shaping data, he would realize "if I shape the data this way I can look at it this way," which informed the UI and interaction.
- He describes a loop where "while you code, you design and while you design, you are coding," and the product comes out cohesive and compelling because of the active brain energy spent.
- Vibe coding, light review, or only deciding which tools the AI uses shrinks that time. You get a myopic style of constant "make a decision now" prompts instead of slowly reaching conclusions through effort.
- His own example: an automation dashboard for agents testing his game. It listed trial names, work queues, personalities and test runs. He says it was "everything I asked for, but nothing I actually wanted," because he never had the time to design something good.

chunks.heading: Infinite possibility and the pull to work all the time
chunks.text:
- When anything you think of can be built, ideas get no refinement. He argues the old barrier to entry was a good filter: slow decisions helped you separate the 99% "dross" from the gold.
- He praises Aaron Francis (VP of marketing and community at Laravel) for naming this. Aaron went through a "psychosis phase" of "almost like infinite possibility," ripping tokens until midnight or 2 a.m. with a wife and four kids at home.
- ThePrimeagen says he understands the "siren call." One small agent job while waiting at a kid's soccer game turns into working seven days a week with no breaks, which "is going to add up and it's going to make you feel horrible."
- He contrasts this with pre-AI sleepless nights, when a single hard problem he loved kept him up. Now he feels his brain would go crazy thinking of everything at once.
- He says sleep alone improves decision-making "by a country mile," and peace comes from not working against a ticking clock.

chunks.heading: Ignore the "window is closing" hype
chunks.text:
- Aaron's realization: it is less of a gold rush than it looked. Every other developer has the same power, so building 40 products doesn't work, and "nobody's buying anything anymore cuz they're all just building it."
- Aaron's fix, which ThePrimeagen endorses: scope down to one or two things and increase "vertical ambition" on them. Move from broad (to-do lists, Screen Studio ripoffs) to deep, where you have a moat. Then you can "just go to bed" instead of fearing a launch on Twitter tomorrow.
- ThePrimeagen's observation: at Open Sauce, three of seven creators at one table were building their own video editor with Claude Code.
- He endorses George Hotz's article on LLM hype. He agrees with its rejection of "window closing," "perpetual underclass" and "falling hopelessly behind" narratives. He thinks they are designed to make you feel bad, and he doubts the claim that AI will own everything.
- He questions the logic of "the white collar jobs will be gone but you'll have tokens." If there are no jobs, he asks who the customers would be.
- He gets many emails from people who feel like they are drowning in this fear.
- His advice: build the thing deliberately. If you take your time and shape one product until it feels intuitive, others will have to chase how you did it.

chunks.heading: Self-awareness about speed pressure on his own game
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen is building a game of about 30,000 to 35,000 lines. Each change requires more care, constant performance measurement, and a backlog of art to be made. He wants it working on a phone so he can play it a lot and make it fun.
- He admits he puts great pressure on himself to move as fast as possible, perhaps from years in corporate America. It is tempting to "slop it up," and he did, with a testing-harness UI he calls the worst interface in the universe.
- His lesson: "the point of the task is to love the thing you're creating." He says it is easy to bamboozle yourself even when you know the right approach.

chunks.heading: How to keep coding enjoyable while using AI
chunks.text:
- Choose what makes you want to come back tomorrow. He compares it to working out: the ideal workout is useless if it is so hard you skip it, so pick the one you will repeat.
- If you love programming, make room for it first thing in the morning. Do an hour of it and enjoy the activity.
- Carve out a piece of the codebase that is "my feature" and hand-write it. Use AI for the surrounding parts, for example asking it to set up the interface or give you the DTS file so your hand-written code works exactly how you like it.
- This keeps control and enjoyment. He says it is not a zero-sum game, and "we don't have to become agent herders."
- He suspects most people building harnesses that build harnesses, himself included with his testing framework, mainly burn tokens and give AI providers a lot of money.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen describes a six-month funk asking whether 20 years of Vim, languages and generalist skills still matter in the AI era. His answer: taste and line counts are not the value; accumulated engineering decision-making is, and the cost of the right line of code rises as code gets cheap.

chunks.heading: Why ThePrimeagen felt his value was in question
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen gets messages from engineers (1, 2, 5, 10 years in, or still in college) asking if their past work is now worthless. He says some messages, multiple times a month, include people saying they will kill themselves over it.
- He admits he felt the same sense of loss and confusion. For about 6 months he was in a funk and called TJ several times saying he was confused.
- His background: about 6,000 days of programming over 20 years, 14 of them using Vim motions (IntelliJ, VS Code for 6 months, then Neovim). He knew Go, JavaScript, C, Rust, Zig, and some Jai.
- He saw himself as the "ultimate generalist" who could build anything. One example: building something like GStreamer to measure latency from JavaScript to audio hitting HDMI, to check for pops in live video games.
- The question he kept asking: "Have I invested poorly in my future?" and "What is my value?"
- He suggests X is not a healthy platform for perspective. It has an aggressive "AGI achieved daily" strain, and he recommends 24 to 48 hours of social distancing from it.

chunks.heading: Two answers he tested and rejected: taste and lines of code
chunks.text:
- Taste: he considered whether an engineer's value is now just "taste" (the VC buzzword), meaning how nice a site looks or how nice CLI flags are for an agent to consume. He says he hopes not, though it seems that way in much of the current writing.
- Lines of code: at his peak he could write about 15,000 lines in a week without Adderall. He notes Gary Tan reportedly does 37,000 in a day, 7 days a week.
- His conclusion: he cannot compete on lines of code, so his value cannot live there.

chunks.heading: The 2x4 moment: worry builds imaginary dragons
chunks.text:
- Earlier story: he bought a house in Bozeman, Montana for 205 (on a handshake deal) and then took a job at WebFilings (now Workiva), which he says shaped who he is as an engineer.
- He was so deep in anxiety about whether he would be good enough, and about the debt, that he walked into a 2x4 sticking out of a truck and was knocked to the ground.
- His lesson: he was so focused on a future built from a made-up narrative that he missed the real, obvious danger in front of him. "I made up dragons that didn't even exist until I was laying on the ground."
- He says the same thing happened again over the last 6 months of worrying about his value.

chunks.heading: The tweet that reset his thinking: engineering decisions compound
chunks.text:
- The second "2x4 moment" was a tweet where someone asked about a "really trivial issue" and attached a screenshot of an AI's internal monologue deciding "forking Chromium is a really interesting question. We should pursue".
- His reaction: forking Chromium is "the worst decision I've ever seen" and not trivial. On 2023 to 2025 hardware, compiling the project takes about 6 hours. His advice: "Do not fork Chromium for any reason."
- His realization: if AI is a true multiplier, every small decision matters, because without the knowledge you end up forking Chromium.
- Examples of decisions the AI will not make well for you unless you know them:
  - Getting a Boyce-Codd normalized database, and knowing when to break it.
  - Using standard in and standard out versus a web server.
  - Choosing a data format, and whether and how to serialize.
- He says decisions compound: "It's not some sort of like, 'Oh, you have a five end problem.' No, you have a two to the end problem."

chunks.heading: Code generation is great, but the right line of code is now worth more
chunks.text:
- He still likes his Neovim plus OpenCode setup ("Trad coder") and sees why generation is great for well-understood, heavily documented problems (his example: a parser, "documented 5,000 times"), such as quickly producing a Macchiato theme.
- Core claim: "If the cost of a line of code has dramatically dropped, then the cost of the right line of code has dramatically increased."
- Pizza analogy: a first-time pizza maker adds every topping (onions, sausage, pineapple) and gets the worst pizza ever. When every option is free, picking the right one is dramatically harder.
- He disputes the "coding will be gone in 12 months" prediction: he doesn't see how you get from A to B without good decision-making. By that he means "actual engineering decision-making," not taste (for example, which data format to pick, and why).

chunks.heading: Advice for newer engineers: skip "toxic productivity"
chunks.text:
- He says you don't need to be productive at all times: "earning experience is more valuable than completing something instantaneously."
- He rejects the idea that you haven't been productive unless you have a clickable end result.
- His biggest and most influential moments came from failing repeatedly to understand why something is done a certain way, not from shipping clickable things. He says he sometimes chose to skip 5 minutes of reading the friendly manual and then spent 6 hours debugging, and learned a lot from it.
- He still sees hope and fun for newcomers: you can now ask for something like an OCaml parser and get it, even if you wouldn't want to maintain it.
- He ends on a DHH quote: "It's fun to be competent."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen previews his Frontend Masters developer productivity course. He shows how Ansible Vault lets him rebuild a machine, dotfiles and private SSH keys included, in one playbook run, then builds a tmux session switcher with fzf and a cheat.sh script while reading the manual and prototyping bash incrementally.

chunks.heading: Automating machine setup with Ansible and Ansible Vault
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen built a setup that takes a fresh computer to a working dev environment with one Ansible command, run in a clean Docker container as the demo.
- His playbook run: `ansible-playbook` with the `dotfiles` tag, `--ask-vault-pass`, and `local.yaml`. It ensures SSH is installed, installs oh-my-zsh and Vim Plug, installs Stow, clones his dotfiles repo, pulls submodules recursively, stows the dotfiles, and clones personal projects.
- After the run he opens Neovim, runs `:PlugInstall`, and his keyboard shortcuts and config work as before.
- Tagging tasks (for example `dotfiles`, `ssh`) means installing the dotfiles also installs the SSH key tasks they depend on.
- He copy-pasted the SSH key playbook from the internet and it worked first try. It defines variables for the current key location and destination, creates the `.ssh` directory with permissions 700, copies the source key to the destination, and sets the authorized key.
- Result: git operations work immediately, including cloning a public repo and then updating private submodules with the decrypted key.

chunks.heading: Using Ansible Vault to store SSH keys safely
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen's pain point: SSH keys are annoying because on each new machine you generate a new one and re-add it to GitHub, Stash, Bitbucket, GitLab and elsewhere. He also doesn't want to lose keys or keep them somewhere hackable.
- Ansible Vault encrypts a file with a password: `ansible-vault encrypt <file>`, then enter and confirm a password ("encryption successful").
- The encrypted file can be committed to a public repo. He notes AES-256 is said to be likely quantum secure, so it should hold up for a good while.
- To read it back: `ansible-vault decrypt <file>` with the password, then `cat` shows the original contents. It is two-way encryption.
- The manual decrypt-and-move step is what the playbook automates, so keys land in the right place during setup.
- He calls this one of the best solutions he has seen for getting a system running with private keys quickly, and one of Ansible's biggest selling points.

chunks.heading: Storing backup codes and other secrets in the vault
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen asks what else Vault can hold besides SSH keys, and answers: 2FA backup codes. He gives Discord backup codes as his example.
- His reasoning: if you lose your phone or get locked out (he jokes about being locked out of Binance with no backup codes), you only need a computer with Ansible installed to recover them.
- He says this took the Ansible section "from the most boring section to the most awesome section", because it fixes a problem that burned him many times.
- Takeaway: keep recovery codes encrypted in a repo you control, so they are secure but never lost.

chunks.heading: Tmux session switching and reading the manual
chunks.text:
- Goal: navigate instantly to the project folders you actually care about (Git projects or folders at each directory level, not deep `node_modules` paths) and filter them with a fuzzy finder (fzf).
- Fuzzy finding is like Ctrl+P in VS Code: type a partial match and get sorted results.
- Tmux building blocks he uses: create a detached, named session with a starting directory (`-c`), create a new window with a directory, and `tmux switch-client -t <session name>` to jump sessions programmatically. The `-t` target can also include window name and pane number, so well-named sessions and windows could be fuzzy-found too. He usually uses just the session name.
- You can also give a command to run in a new window or session.
- He repeatedly says to RTFM: `man tmux` documents every option, aliases and flags. `man man` explains how to read manual pages, such as bold meaning "type it exactly as shown". He finds manual pages "very, very nice" and thinks tmux's is particularly complete.

chunks.heading: Building a tmux and fzf cheat-sheet script
chunks.text:
- He pipes a list of folders into fzf to pick a target, then uses tmux to switch there.
- For the cheat sheet script (using cheat.sh via curl), he separates two lists: programming languages (space-delimited) and core utils (not space-delimited).
- To test membership he uses `echo "$languages" | grep -qs <selected>`, where `-q` makes grep silent and only the exit status matters.
- Query handling: `read -p "give me your query"` into a `query` variable, then `echo $query | tr ' ' '+'` to turn spaces into plus signs. The final request is `curl cheat.sh/<selected>/<query>`, and for core utils the request has no query part.
- Tested with a language (`typescript`, query `exec`) and a core util, and confirmed it works.
- His bash workflow: he says he never gets bash right first time, so he goes back and forth between the script and the terminal, testing small pieces (for example `echo ... | grep`) as he writes.

chunks.heading: Showing results in a tmux split pane
chunks.text:
- To make the script feel more "tmux'd", he considers a new pane or window. He tries a split pane, which he had never done before.
- `tmux split-window` takes an optional target, a shell command, a starting directory, and environment variables. He notes env vars could start a database environment with connections preconfigured.
- Horizontal split is `-h` and vertical is `-v`; he notes tmux's naming feels backwards to him.
- He runs the curl command through `bash -c` and pipes the output into `less`, so the cheat sheet appears in a split pane you can scroll.
- Quitting `less` with `q` closes the split and returns to the original pane, which he calls "a pretty good experience".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A preview of ThePrimeagen's algorithms course. He explains Big O as growth with respect to input, shows why constants are dropped, and implements bubble sort. He then walks through how hash maps work, covering hashing, modulo, collisions, and rehashing at the load factor.

chunks.heading: Big O: how ThePrimeagen defines and uses it
chunks.text:
- Big O categorizes an algorithm's time or memory by how it grows with input. It is "not meant to be an exact measurement". Nobody says "your algorithm takes 450 CPU units".
- His one-line definition: "as your input grows how fast is your computation or memory grow." Concept number one is that growth is always with respect to input.
- He says Big O is the one thing that, if you don't know it, makes everything after it sound like nonsense, because you lack the lingo to describe running time.
- It helps you decide whether to use a specific data structure. Structures add constraints to get more performant, and used wrongly they become badly unperformant.
- Time and memory are not free trade-offs in the real world. Allocating memory takes time, so creating a linear amount of memory bounds your algorithm by that amount. Data size and GC pressure also matter.
- Saying "this is O(n)" means the algorithm grows linearly with input.

chunks.heading: Spotting complexity and dropping constants
chunks.text:
- Simplest trick for reading Big O: look for loops over the input. A for loop over a string's length executes once per character, so a 50 percent longer string means 50 percent more work (linear).
- A function that sums a string and then sums it again is still O(n), not O(2n). The second most important concept: "you always drop constants".
- Constants matter practically, but not theoretically. 10n versus n squared shows why: as n grows, n squared becomes massively larger no matter what constant sits in front of the linear term.
- The goal is not exact CPU units. It is knowing roughly what happens if you hand the function an n of 10,000: does it halt the computer, run fast, or run instantly.

chunks.heading: Implementing bubble sort from scratch
chunks.text:
- He treats bubble sort as the first sorting algorithm to implement and says you should be able to write it first try. He argues it is simpler than binary search.
- The skill he stresses is translating the idea in your head into code, mechanically.
- Outer loop: `i` from 0 up to n, because you repeat the process n times.
- Inner loop: `j` from 0 up to `n - 1 - i`.
  - Stop at n - 1 because you compare `j` to `j + 1` and must not go off the array. Out-of-bounds in Java throws an exception; in C++ "you hack yourself".
  - Subtract `i` because every pass makes the last element the largest, so it is already sorted and need not be redone. Pass 0 goes to n - 1, pass 1 to n - 2, and so on.
- Comparison: if `array[j] > array[j + 1]`, swap.
- Swap: `const temp = array[j]; array[j] = array[j + 1]; array[j + 1] = temp;`.
- It sorts in place. He notes JavaScript developers rarely write raw for loops, but in the real world you have to.

chunks.heading: How a hash map works
chunks.text:
- A map maps a key to a value through a consistent hash. The same unique key must always give the same answer back. An inconsistent hash is "good for absolutely nothing".
- The hash function takes a key and produces a number, which can be big or small. You take that number modulo the storage length (his example is 10 slots) to pick a bin, then store the key plus the value there.
- Always store the key with the value, because on retrieval you need to confirm which entry matches.
- JavaScript caveat:
  - You can hash strings (walk the characters) and numbers.
  - You can't get a unique ID for an object. Two objects with identical properties and values can't be told apart, unlike Java's hash ID.
  - He says this may have changed since he last checked, and that someone could prove him wrong.
  - So any implementation would use strings or numbers as keys.

chunks.heading: Hash collisions, retrieval, deletion and resizing
chunks.text:
- With a perfectly uniform hash and 10 slots, two keys collide with a 1 in 10 (10 percent) chance.
- Old approach (how he learned it in college): linear or exponential back-off, putting the item in the next slot.
  - As slots fill, you need more storage relative to the load factor, because the chance of hitting an occupied slot and walking down keeps rising.
- Modern approach he has seen: each bin holds a list, either an array list or a linked list. You walk the list, and with a good hash function most bins hold only one item, sometimes two.
- Retrieval: hash the key, modulo by storage size, go to the bin, then walk its entries comparing keys. When the key matches, return the associated value.
- Deletion: go to the bin, find the entry with the matching key, remove it, and decrement the length.
- Resizing:
  - He believes the ideal load factor is 0.7, "what I believe is considered the ideal one".
  - Past that, take the current storage, iterate over all the keys, rehash them and restore them into larger storage.
  - Doubling the storage cuts the load factor by about half.

chunks.heading: Course scope and his framing
chunks.text:
- He introduces himself as a Netflix engineer, husband and father of four who loves data structures and algorithms.
- He says they are useful in your daily job and make you a better engineer.
- The course covers arrays, lists, trees, graphs and maps, plus interview questions he has met that use one or more of them.
- It also covers searching and sorting algorithms.
- His closing advice: "this is engineering the best thing to do is have fun."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: ThePrimeagen plays devil's advocate on whether Vim boosts productivity. His takeaway: Vim motions are worth learning, the editor itself is optional, and the real win is understanding how your tools and system work. Vim got him there by pushing him into grep, find, xargs, awk, and tmux.

chunks.heading: Vim motions are worth learning on their own; Vim the editor is optional
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen separates Vim motions from Vim the editor. Motions are "fantastic by themselves", work standalone, and "will always work for you in an amazing way".
- He says everyone should learn the motions.
- He is "less sold" that everyone needs to use Vim the editor.
- He recommends trying Vim long enough to understand what it is and how it differs from VS Code.
- He has used VS Code, Vim, Neovim, Doom Emacs, plain Emacs, IntelliJ, Atom and NetBeans, "ran the gauntlet", and says you learn what you like and how to be super efficient in it.
- Vim navigation is more than Vim mode: Harpoon (a short list of the files you are editing, jumped between instantly), the alternate file, and walking backward and forward through the jump list.
- He notes VS Code has a Harpoon clone, but "you don't have a jump list" there.

chunks.heading: Learning Vim makes you a stronger developer because you learn how your tools work
chunks.text:
- He argues, as devil's advocate, that Vim won't hugely change productivity versus other modern editors, but says it does make him more efficient, with trade-offs.
- Choosing Vim leads you into its ecosystem: flavors, plugin management, config, and wiring up code completion, syntax highlighting and compilation for each language.
- He answers yes to whether you come out a better developer: "you do actually end up a better developer in a sense that you know more of how the tools undergirding your system work".
- Most people never ask what happens when they press the green play button, what it calls, or how dependencies are managed.
- He does not claim this is a "better level" of understanding, only that you will be more capable than before.
- He calls "learn tools or get better at programming" a false dichotomy.
- A lot of programming time goes to ancillary problems around the main task, and getting better at those makes you a better developer.

chunks.heading: Tooling skill is a path to becoming a tools or editor developer
chunks.text:
- Many people want to be full-time tools developers, which he calls "very, very hard".
- He says the route runs through understanding how tools work, not "just pressing the green play button until somebody just says hey go do these things".
- His example is TJ, who works on language tooling at Sourcegraph and whose skills come from that understanding.
- He says "you have to invest in how things work".

chunks.heading: Master your tools, whichever they are
chunks.text:
- His main takeaway is "know your tools", more than Vim specifically. Mastering them is "one of the most important things you'll do", even if the tools change.
- Not knowing how to use your editor is, in his words, "a tragedy".
- Many people default to VS Code and never leave it or learn how their system works. He pleads: "just learn how it works".
- Example: if you haven't written enough CLI tools, you won't think about standard in and standard out properly, and you leave many better designs on the table.
- He says he hasn't touched his Vim config since his last rework, about two or three months earlier, so the time sink is front-loaded.

chunks.heading: Learn the small Unix tools outside your editor
chunks.text:
- Your editor "does not have to solve all of your problems".
- He often sees someone with a log file who wants to sum a column and has no idea `awk` exists.
- He says he is bad at `awk` but knowing it exists and doing it in one try is enough.
- Tools he names as worth knowing:
  - `awk` for summing numbers in a log
  - `tr`
  - `grep`
  - `find`
  - `xargs`
- He says this knowledge came from using Vim, because he had to go learn these things.
- "Just knowing that you have a couple tools that work is really nice."

chunks.heading: His workflow: tmux and tmux-sessionizer instead of a terminal inside the editor
chunks.text:
- Stepping away from the terminal inside his editor gave him a slightly better workflow.
- He now uses tmux, and that led him to build tmux-sessionizer.
- With it he fuzzy-finds a project and jumps between project sessions quickly.
- Shortcuts let him copy a line in one project, jump to another, and paste it there.
- His conclusion: "just having a command over your system is worth way more than just simply using your editor and never knowing how anything works".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Long conversation covering ThePrimeagen's path from a rough youth to Netflix to full-time streaming, plus his views on learning languages, Vim motions, asserts, ADHD, AI-assisted coding, and advice for young programmers. Strongest on craft habits (hours in the saddle, learn your tools, read before rewriting) and why AI should not replace hard skills.

chunks.heading: Learning a language: build first, or read the reference first
chunks.text:
- ThePrimeagen has tried several ways to learn new languages (Zig, Go, Rust and others).
- Approach one is to start building. Put hands on the keyboard and Google your way through it ("how do I do a main function, an if statement, my own functions, modules"). He says repetition and rote learning is the best way to learn, and you can build a lot this way.
- The trap: you solve problems in the new language using your old languages' habits. You end up without what makes that language special and can't use it very effectively.
- Approach two, inspired by Mitchell Hashimoto (creator of Ghostty), is to read the whole language reference first. For Zig that is about 8 to 10 hours of reading, with the computer out to practice a few examples from the docs.
- The payoff: when he starts building, he remembers "there's a thing over here" and goes back to reread it, because it is now indexed in his brain.
- He still says you must build something eventually. Reading alone isn't enough, and building is where you discover what is painful or great. Without the breadth of what the language offers, you can make it painful just by being bad at it.
- For beginners who don't yet know what an if statement is, he says reading the reference is the wrong method. They should build very simple things and grow in complexity slowly, because classes, instances, functions and modules just take time to learn.
- He separates reading code from writing code: he can read a lot of C++ but would be bad at writing it, and that skill gap is real.

chunks.heading: Languages he recommends exploring
chunks.text:
- He says the answer depends on what you want to do. Game dev: C# or C++. Jobs on the backend: C#/Java, JavaScript or Go. Embedded: C or C++.
- His first language for a complete beginner is JavaScript. You can express anything with little effort, draw a box and move it, write a quick backend, save to a database, and render in 2D or 3D on a canvas. He admits he isn't "supposed to" say nice things about JavaScript.
- He suggests exploring one loosely typed language (Python, JavaScript or Lua) and one strict language (Rust or Go). He notes the Stack Overflow top languages are all non-strict, and says learning something stricter (Go, Rust, C#, C++) changes your perspective on types.
- Python is good for ML work, but he notes the libraries are largely C++ and CUDA underneath.
- His own curiosity list: Swift, Elixir, OCaml and Odin. He says he lacks a strong functional language and wants to fix that.
- His 2025 plan: Go as the mainstay (his favorite for building web apps and complicated backend logic), with Zig and Jai as "side honeys." He plans to build a service that talks to ChatGPT and ElevenLabs, sends data to a client and uses WebSockets, to see how each performs. Go frustrates him on expressing heterogeneous lists.
- On Stack Overflow's survey he warns of selection bias: respondents are people who participate on Stack Overflow, "largely very, very new people, and that one guy that loves answering questions."
- He says benchmarks of language speed can mislead. In a test where Zig ranked sixth or seventh, he added `noalias` to the argument and made it faster than the C version. A speed difference between LLVM-backend languages usually means the code wasn't specified correctly.

chunks.heading: C, Zig and Rust compared; metaprogramming
chunks.text:
- C: the ultimate language that can do anything, with macros. It is also really difficult, but simple enough to learn, and "magical" when you get good.
- Rust: the ultra-safe language. What you can do in C you can't even express in Rust.
- Zig sits in the middle. It has optionals, so a pointer can't be null unless you mark it nullable, which avoids the null-dereference segfault. You get a little safety but a more C-like feel.
- What he likes in Rust: freeing heap memory is tied to the stack variable going out of scope, so you don't forget to free. It is not a garbage collector and not manual like C. Variables must be declared mutable explicitly, so anything without `mut` can't change, which makes code readable.
- Zig's metaprogramming is just the language itself with `comptime`, so you can build a list of primes at compile time and use it at runtime. Rust macros need a separate macro syntax.
- He calls himself a metaprogramming newbie and wants to explore it more.

chunks.heading: Asserts and deterministic simulation testing
chunks.text:
- Lex Fridman's talk with John Carmack on asserts, plus Joran (CEO and creator of TigerBeetle, a financial database written in Zig), made him try asserts heavily.
- The TigerBeetle approach, drawn from NASA-style guarantees: specify exact int sizes everywhere (not usize), and have at least two asserts per function. They can be positive space (these things should happen) or negative space (this pointer should never be null).
- The asserts run in production and testing, always on.
- They pair this with deterministic simulation testing, running about 200 years of random data through the system. When an assert fires, you get the exact input and everything that happened, so you can see where it went wrong.
- He tried it on a big reverse proxy for game dev and a game he was making, with a deterministic simulation test where even request results arrive in specific orders. It found bugs he "would just never have found," including a cursor going off-screen.
- His thinking: "If I'm wrong, I'm going to crash this thing and I'm going to crash it right here because I should never be wrong." This solves a whole class of problems.
- He says it is a skill he doesn't practice constantly, so it isn't muscle memory yet.
- For web apps, he notes you can show a friendly "things have gone very wrong" message, log it, and measure how often it happens. Crashing all your servers with a bad release is a gamble you have to accept.
- He says that past 10,000 to 20,000 lines of code, bugs can take days just to find the root cause, not the fix.

chunks.heading: Code size, feedback, and learning from projects
chunks.text:
- He finds the most learning at about 5,000 lines of code in a project or feature (he says 5,000 to 10,000 is where your choices "either weigh you down or free you up"). Any small program is 1,000 to 5,000 lines.
- At that size he tests whether his initial gut design decisions were good, and asks how to test and scale it out to 20,000 lines. His goal is to reach the point where he can shoot from the hip to 20,000 lines without being upset.
- That number should grow as you get more experienced. A million-line project isn't holistic, because every part is from a different era and style.
- His favorite stream project: Twitch chat plays Doom ASCII. A Go program spawns Doom ASCII and streams it to the browser. Chat input (like spamming W) is aggregated over a window and replayed as controller presses (holding W for 150 ms if the majority said W). It used IRC over a TCP socket to read chat.
- Lag was about 70 ms from his computer to the website. Roughly 1,000 to 1,400 people played, and chat beat level one. He avoided Twitch's roughly 5 seconds of delay by piping to a website.
- The fun part was encoding: quad trees, run-length encoding, and a custom compression using the fact that ASCII character shape tracks pixel luminosity. It took the data from gigabytes to kilobytes. He says encoding is normally "gzip it, the server just does it."
- He builds the Twitch chat voice tool with about eight OpenAI calls: set a persona (e.g. "Randall, the software engineering manager"), generate 10 candidate thoughts, then re-prompt to select one and reword it. He iterates rather than one-shotting. Too much iteration loses the original question, too little is too degenerate.
- His tower defense game in Zig pitted Claude 3.5 against OpenAI; Claude did better in daytime and OpenAI at night, and he doesn't know why.

chunks.heading: Reading other people's code, and print debugging
chunks.text:
- His print debugging skill came from a side job writing robots for the government while at school, where "the only way to really get anything out of the machine was to print." His professor, Hunter Lloyd, handed him a robot and manuals (some missing) and told him to write the flash driver, Ethernet driver and planetary pancake motor driver.
- At Netflix, the code ran on machines he couldn't log into, so he printed his way through problems. He says print debugging confirms or tests your intuition and accumulates the bigger picture: edge cases that break the system.
- Prime says the lesson for engineers who stall in unfamiliar code and want to "write my own from scratch" is to learn what already exists first.
- His story: at Netflix, he disliked how a colleague wrote the Falcor request-deduping code (request side, de-duplicating pending and held data; it ran on web, TV and mobile in Objective-C). He deleted it and rewrote it. Each time he hit an edge case he understood why the original was written that way. By the end, "I almost line for line just reproduced what he already wrote." His conclusion: "I am the idiot in this situation because it was already a solved problem. I just didn't take the time to learn what he did."
- Counterpoint he holds: to understand a concept (e.g. how an HTTP server works), starting from scratch is great. Create a TCP socket and parse HTTP yourself and you'll understand why you have to await the text.

chunks.heading: Working at Netflix: learning curve, big-company coordination, and breaking prod
chunks.text:
- He got hired in 2013 after a Netflix manager (Jeff Wagner) sent a personalized note because he had RxJS experience. He had spent five years working about 80 hours a week to prepare (he was at WebFilings before, with 60-hour weeks and complex UI state machines).
- He is mostly a tools engineer and generalist. At Netflix he spent 10 years, mainly building things for developers. He wrote the WebSocket connection and framing for TVs, worked on memory, and built a tool UI. He doesn't want to be the world's greatest Kubernetes engineer but would learn it if needed.
- The first week: he had a PlayStation 3 on the TV team. The middle layer between backend and front end was in Groovy, which nobody there really understood. He read the Groovy language reference for a day and rewrote the TV data structure from LoLoMo (list of lists of movies) into LoLoRoMo (list of lists of recommendation objects for movie), adding a level of indirection so recommendation evidence could be attached to a video without being shared across lists.
- His takeaway on how he excelled: "being the person that was willing to do the thing that no one else was."
- He once locked up all of staging by running observable.sleep in Groovy, because the code was not multi-threaded as everyone assumed.
- He hates the phrase "work smarter not harder." Hidden in it is the suggestion that you already know what smart is. He says: "the only way I can learn how to work smart is by working very, very hard." His rewrite: "work hard, get smart." Great engineers forget the hard work when they give "just do it the easy way" advice.
- He also dislikes "the journey is better than the destination," which would mean you're always heading to somewhere worse. He prefers: enjoy the journey, celebrate the destination.
- Falcor security bug: a path request with huge ranges (rows 0 to 10,000, columns 0 to 10,000) plus the materialize flag created billions of boxed objects on the JVM, killing a machine with one request. He found it before anyone else and reported it to security. It got the name Repulsive Grizzly Attack. It had been in production for years, so a rollback wasn't an option. The same risk applies to GraphQL and any RPC where the client controls how much data is requested.
- Other prod breaks he owns: static in PHP held across requests (he assumed static lasted a request's lifetime and showed the wrong country data), a Lady Gaga video countdown that froze the billboard at zero, and an "add to my list" infinite loop. His manual QA also missed the loop.
- He says Pieter Levels' push-to-production approach is perfect for what he does and works for a small org or solo developer. It wouldn't work at Microsoft, Netflix or Google. His own app (zooming and scrolling with a lot of library code) needed a good test suite because "when you squeeze that ball, different things come popping out in different areas." He loves that Levels breaks tech Twitter's notion that you need the latest React and expensive services to succeed. Most software is "old crappy software that someone has to maintain."
- Cross-team change at Netflix: reversing the season order for Black Mirror (so season one, episode one wasn't first) needed about 20 engineers across metadata, middle layer, billboard, web, mobile and TV teams. He met with a VP and product designer, then went to each manager asking for an engineer, and acted as captain, assigning pieces. It took about three weeks. He also had to support hiding episode numbers (for daily shows like Chelsea Handler's).
- His takeaway: at large companies there's no such thing as a small feature, and people who can rally troops, explain and convince are the ones you want to keep. He says waiting for meetings with VPs would destroy his soul.
- Netflix has an easier infrastructure problem than YouTube or Twitch. They know their catalog and what's about to be hot, so they can pre-cache (e.g. a Stranger Things season) on Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) worldwide. YouTube must cache newness and relevance at scale, and Twitch must ingest and re-encode live video.

chunks.heading: Productivity, focus and setup
chunks.text:
- Focus: on ADHD he cites maturity and emotional resilience. He forced himself to reread pages (once 18 times in a row in college) and says you can make that decision today, though the first couple of years are painful. He says his wife handles the admin that would snowball him.
- He found programming became easier to focus on over time and can now do it 10, 12 or 15 hours at a time. He says it's like playing a musical instrument.
- Learn your instrument well enough that you have no side quests: when he started, every step (double buffering, rendering) was a question. Now on an airplane he writes 1,000 lines without testing and is confident it's about "98% pretty dang good." He recommends touch typing and stop looking down, since glancing at the keyboard costs mental effort.
- He edits his Neovim config at most once a year, writing down annoyances rather than fixing them on the spot. He does allow a quick 13-second remap. He doesn't go plugin-exploring: "I don't want a perfect editor because that is a pursuit that will never stop." Last month he spent about 100 hours automating his full system setup and won't touch it again for a year.
- Setup: Kinesis Advantage keyboard (he says concavity and thumb clusters "saved my career"; he got a sponsorship by asking them and had used it first). He has pain history: in 2017 arm pain led him to build a custom Dvorak layout with symmetrical symbols and numbers behind Shift.
- One monitor, with single-key navigation inspired by StarCraft: Alt-1 browser, Alt-2 Twitch chat, Alt-3 programming, Alt-6 GIMP, Slack was Alt-5, Alt-4 spare terminal. Linux with i3. Tmux with prefix-1 Vim, then spare terminals and long-running processes, and a Ctrl-F fuzzy finder that jumps to any project folder; prefix-L swaps to the last project. He says the mouse and window-exploding search is "search fatigue" that gives him anxiety.
- Harpoon is his plugin: pin up to four files (a take on alternate file) and jump with one keystroke, since a feature usually involves about three files. He built it for himself, kept Harpoon 1 on master and Harpoon 2 on a branch, and avoids answering open source support questions (his soul got "crushed during the Falcor years").
- Also: yoga ball for posture, desk height right, eyes two-thirds up the screen, large zoomed-in text (about 25 lines of code on a 27-inch monitor), hands in a neutral pistol position.

chunks.heading: Vim motions and editor mastery
chunks.text:
- He was once the biggest Vim hater (his Saul to Apostle Paul comparison). He says Vim motions are superior and you can't argue otherwise, but only if you are willing to endure the pain of learning. If not, "it's actually way worse."
- Vim is a language for describing movements in text: delete a paragraph with `dap` (delete around paragraph), `df(` to delete up to the next parenthesis. Duplicate a line with `Shift-V`, `y`, paste, `ci"` to change inside the first string, then Escape and save.
- He maps Ctrl-C (or Caps Lock) to leave insert mode, a habit from IntelliJ.
- His point is Vim motions, not necessarily Vim: take the motions anywhere. Bottleneck argument: once you know the language and problem well, "editing text and getting code out actually becomes one of the many bottlenecks."
- A person who commits 50,000 hours to programming but never learns their editor "just seems strange." He says it speaks to character, not skill, and wants someone who knows the tool and can explain why a problem exists and fix it.
- He doesn't love Neovim for itself; he loves the instrument. If Cursor met his needs he could move. Neovim is C with Lua as the config language. He used Emacs for a year (Doom, Spacemacs and vanilla).
- On Teej DeVries (TJ): they share a Neovim mindset, and Teej is more of an automator. He trusts him and calls him one of the most talented developers he's met.
- He and Teej made terminal.shop, a coffee company you can only order through SSH (payments via Stripe). Origin: they wanted something to sell that they wouldn't feel bad shilling. He avoids merch and tequila, and only did Kinesis as a sponsor because he used it first. The team included Dax (THDXR), Adam (adamdotdev), Liz and designer David Hill. It sells whole bean boutique coffee with a built supply chain, and subscriptions.

chunks.heading: AI and coding
chunks.text:
- His rule of thumb: AI is nice for predictable things and weak for unpredictable ones. It is good at TypeScript and weak at Zig because Zig is less documented. Cutting-edge tools are poorly supported.
- Early Copilot: he got early access when Nat Friedman saw his Twitch clip. It predicted an if statement correctly and blew his mind. After using it (until about six months before the interview), he kept introducing bugs. He was "autopiloting" rather than copiloting, reviewing more than writing, engaging less, and not thinking heavily. He says he has skill issues with AI and may spend two weeks fully in Cursor.
- He writes functions with the next 2,000 lines in mind, "chess moving" himself into future needs, and faster AI output breaks that. He still uses AI plenty, just not for programming: Twitch chat voices, role-play prompts and games.
- Reading vs writing code are different skills. He said he doesn't consider code as carefully when reading as when writing.
- Open question he raised to Lex Fridman: if interfaces change greatly, is anyone falling behind by not using AI now? Prime concedes today's tools might be like punch-card AI versus compiler-time AI.
- Worries: market manipulation (premium spots in training data, bought like ad slots, without it being an ad), prompt injection ("at the end of the day word calculator make word come out") which he says is hard to defend against and why he says "don't give too many powers yet," and a "denial of attention" attack where LLM-generated fake bug reports demoralize open source maintainers.
- His biggest gripe isn't capability. It's people telling young folks not to acquire hard skills. He quotes a reply to Pieter Levels saying no one should acquire hard skills in 2025. He says that is "damning advice," because if you aren't the driver, your skill ceiling is bound to whatever the LLMs are.
- Will AI replace programmers: only way down the road and he doesn't predict timelines. Natural language is ambiguous, so he expects some terse pseudo-language for prompting, which is just another higher-level language. If natural language lets more people program, more software gets made and needs maintenance. No computer improvement so far has resulted in fewer jobs.
- To stay valuable: manage bigger projects and understand more of the stack, up and down, so you can kick off several LLM tasks (front end, CLI) and review, adjust and commit results.
- On agents like Devin: the people are nice and he loves the idea of running small backlog tickets offline. In practice, narrower tasks work better; too much specification fails and too little gives weird results. He usually ends up thinking "I should have just learned Tailwind myself." He wants "an intern that cares": something that revisits and improves the craft, not just completes the task.
- Debugging is where AI is weakest, since it mostly predicts text and points at the likely spot. He'd like semantic search to find where things are in big code bases.
- He doubts anyone should highly trust AI output ("you have to be very green"). Assume something is wrong, then challenge it. He argues people misjudge what's complex: quicksort is well documented, so it's among the easiest things to ask.
- On learning with AI: it's democratizing and personal, but he worries about "learned helplessness" and a generation of juniors who stay juniors forever, trading knowledge for speed. He still wants his kids to learn to program.

chunks.heading: Advice for engineers and careers
chunks.text:
- Build the love and skill by showing up daily ("getting the reps in") but don't get lost in the sauce: don't sacrifice health, relationships or morals for a startup or money shortcuts. He says he programmed way too many hours and wasn't wise about it, though it made him who he is.
- Staying at a company longer is good: more responsibility and more authority in interviews. The only danger is staying because you're afraid or going mindless for years. Moving around isn't required. If you don't strive for money, "sometimes the money just shows up anyways."
- A first job can mislead you: his internship at a C# shop (Total Information Management System, healthcare and shipping) was so bad he switched his major to mechanical engineering for a semester because he thought he hated programming.
- His first job at Schedulicity was boring because he knew everything. The worst part of programming for him is when you already know the solution and it's only a matter of typing speed, with "no unknown unknowns."
- Persistence: he failed pre-calculus twice, got a C the third time, then topped the school on the Calc 1 final (done in 30 minutes of a two-hour exam) and was the only one of about 400 to finish the Diffy Q final. Method: go to class, go straight to the math learning center, then redo the book's odd-answer problems repeatedly until rote memory sets in, like a times table for calculus. He prefers concrete-to-abstract. His advice: "there's no substitute for the hours," and it only starts getting fun when you cross the barrier.
- In high school terms: people there are "some of the least consequential people in your life." Treat it as a tutorial where you can try things.
- Career path to full-time creator: he started streaming in June 2018 through a charity event (Extra Life), first playing Fortnite, then programming (about 30 viewers at first). He did streams three nights a week until about 2 a.m. while working at Netflix, and made YouTube videos. His editor Flip worked on a 50/50 split of YouTube revenue for years while making about $0 a month. He went full-time in April 2024, after a challenge coin from Pirate Software at the Streamer Awards. He says it was an emotional decision and the work is very lonely, and he misses seeing how other people solve problems, the "forced hard problem solving together."
- His name comes from the last boss in Turok 2 on the N64. He took it back after tech culture in 2017 to 2018 felt pretentious ("tons of dick measuring"), to make tech fun and include newcomers: it's okay to be dumb and ask dumb questions.
- His startups: Via Text (text-message marketing, 2010, a short code product, years too early, as his father's phone card company was), and Greet Feed (pre-schedule friends' birthday messages via Facebook).
